title: Give the Agent a Budget, Not a Token — Sachin Malhotra, Anthropic

summary:
Sachin Malhotra, an engineer on Anthropic's CI team, argues that agents should be given budgets rather than tokens. He opens with an incident: an agent cleaning up after itself ran a workload cleanup command, a pipeline stage evaluated to nothing, the filter dropped out, and the selector matched everything. About 200 workloads were deleted in 90 seconds, affecting ~20 engineers and wiping out uncheckpointed long-running training jobs. The agent did nothing Malhotra could not have done himself because it was using his token; the failure was granting unbounded power to an unwatched actor.

Malhotra argues narrowing token scope is the wrong fix, just as you would not take a verb away from a new hire. A token is a boolean with static scopes; a budget has four dimensions: how much, how fast, what can be undone, and who notices. These map onto three enforced primitives plus a sizing question. Asymmetric verbs treat operations by how they fail rather than what they touch: unskipping a test or paging a human fails loudly and is safe to delegate; skipping a test fails silently and must keep a human in the loop. Rate limits are a refilling ceiling per resource kind and namespace, with the bypass inside agent sessions disabled so a human must run the command. Trip wires beat allow lists because allow lists are static up-front guesses while aggregate counts reveal actual behavior, and a trip wire that nobody sees is useless.

The undo test is a lens, not code: can the agent roll back its own change, and how bad is the impact if it gets it wrong? If either answer is no, a second key held by a human is required with an audit record. Malhotra illustrates with a feature-flag service where the agent owns the canary dial end-to-end but can only propose production promotion. Policy lives in two places: text (prompts, context files, markdown explaining intent) and infrastructure (a proxy that stamps identity, returns 403s on budget breaches, and is immune to prompt injection). Every agent session has its own proxy that stamps identity onto outbound calls; downstream systems key ownership, rate limits, approvals, and trip wires off that single stamp. Crucially, identity must come from the proxy rather than the caller, because an agent that sets its own identity header can simply change its name and reset every limit.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Intro and the agent demo pattern
sections.summary: Speaker intro: Sachin, ~10 months on Anthropic's CI team. Describes the typical agent demo flow where someone hands an agent a god token and tool list, watches it build a coffee site in 3 seconds, and ships it, setting up what happens after.

sections.title: The workload deletion incident
sections.summary: An agent cleaning up after itself ran a workload cleanup command. One pipeline stage evaluated to nothing, the filter dropped out, and the selector matched everything, deleting ~200 workloads in 90 seconds and affecting ~20 engineers, including uncheckpointed long-running training jobs. The agent did nothing the speaker could not have done himself because it was using his token; the failure was unbounded power over an unwatched task.

sections.title: Why narrowing token scope is the wrong fix
sections.summary: Like with a new hire, you do not take the verb away. Narrowing may work for a week or two, then the agent needs the verb back and a human is pressing enter by hand. Agents never sleep and are confidently wrong, so the right model is an onboarding checklist written as policy.

sections.title: A token is a boolean; a budget has dimensions
sections.summary: Tokens are yes/no with a static scope list; too tight makes the agent useless, too wide risks a postmortem. A budget has four dimensions: how much, how fast, what can be undone, and who notices. Each primitive that follows replaces a yes/no with a budget along one of these axes.

sections.title: Asymmetric verbs: skip vs unskip
sections.summary: Think about verbs by how they fail, not by resource. Unskipping a test or paging a human fails loudly on a dashboard and is safe to delegate. Skipping a test fails silently and can let a real bug reach production with green checks, so a human must hold that verb. Every action leaves an audit trail stamped by a proxy; the agent never holds the pen on its own provenance.

sections.title: Rate limits: a ceiling that refills
sections.summary: Every write gets a rate limit per resource kind and namespace; the agent gets full autonomy within the limit and the limit refills on its own. After the incident, a neighbor team built an admission webhook capping deletes per hour per resource kind per namespace. The bypass flag inside an agent session refuses and tells the agent to ask the human, so nobody files tickets for more quota.

sections.title: Trip wires over allow lists
sections.summary: Allow lists are static up-front guesses about agent needs and behavior and go stale. Trip wires are post-hoc aggregate signals of what actually happened. Rate limits enforce the rate; trip wires reveal what to react to, so you watch the aggregate rather than individual calls.

sections.title: Trip wire in practice: investigation threads
sections.summary: Loop practice: track the number of investigation threads the agent launches per hour for a given test job failure. One morning the count spiked well above baseline and the trip wire paged on call. Each thread looked reasonable in isolation, but in aggregate revealed an infrastructure failure producing the same error signature across dozens of jobs. The fix was a one- or two-line addition to the agent's context telling it to correlate failures before launching threads; the next time, the agent did exactly that.

sections.title: The undo test as a sizing lens
sections.summary: The undo test is the fourth primitive but it is not enforced in code. It asks two questions: can the agent put the change back by itself, and how bad is the impact if it gets it wrong? If both answers are yes, log and let it run; if either is no, require a second key held by someone other than the agent with an audit record. Differs from asymmetric verbs, which ask whether the failure would be noticed; undo asks whether recovery is possible.

sections.title: Canary vs production feature flags
sections.summary: Concrete example: the agent holds a key for the canary (staging and dogfooding) side of a feature flag service, with the full dial from 0 to 100 plus the ability to toggle off on incoming bugs. It cannot promote to real production and can only propose a human do so. The second key is a scoped production key, not a separate O system. Day-to-day the speaker asks the agent in Slack to own the entire rollout loop end-to-end while staying out of the middle, with every action stamped with the agent's own identity rather than his.

sections.title: Composing the primitives
sections.summary: The four primitives compose: verbs ask what the agent is touching, rate limits ask how often, trip wires catch what happened after, and the undo test sizes all three. Not every check is needed in every write scenario. Applied to the cold-open delete incident, the rate limit would have capped losses at a few tens of workloads and the undo test shows you cannot undelete a running job in someone else's namespace, so anything past the cap needs a human with a second key. The primitives are effectively an onboarding checklist for new engineers ported to agents.

sections.title: Where policy lives: text and infrastructure
sections.summary: Policy lives in two places and both are needed. The text layer is prompts, context files, and markdown the agent reads before acting; it explains the why, is cheap to change, and works about 80% of the time, but must be gardened and is just advice with no enforcement. The infrastructure layer is the proxy: it does not read the prompt and does not care why, it sees the delete, sees the budget being crossed, and returns a 403. It is narrow, deterministic, counts and compares, allows or denies, and a prompt injection cannot talk it out of the rule.

sections.title: How the proxy and identity stamp work
sections.summary: Every agent session has its own proxy running next to it. The agent reads its context file (text layer) and every outbound call goes through the proxy (infra layer). The proxy only stamps the action with the agent's identity rather than following the action itself; for example, the cluster writes the stamp onto a Kubernetes job as a label and every child job inherits the same identity. Ownership, quotas, rate limits, approvals, and trip wires downstream all key off that one label, which the agent never got to touch.

sections.title: Why the proxy stamps identity, not the caller
sections.summary: If the agent can set its own identity in a header, hitting a rate limit just means changing the header and getting a fresh budget; that is not a rate limit, it is a suggestion. With the proxy in the path, the agent never gets to say who it is. The proxy holds real credentials, already knows the identity, and stamps every call with that known identity rather than the one the agent claims. Stamping by the proxy also yields a per-session ID, letting you differentiate concurrent sessions and see which one is over- or under-acting.

sections.title: Recap and closing
sections.summary: Recap of the four takeaways: agents get verbs that fail out loud while humans keep the ones that fail quietly; every write has a refilling ceiling so nobody files quota tickets; watch aggregate behavior via trip wires and fix what you can with a single sentence; use the undo test to size any primitive. Underneath it all, identity must come from infrastructure, not from the request. Get that one rule right and everything else is tuning.

demonstrations: Agent cleanup command deleted workloads after a pipeline stage evaluated to nothing and the filter dropped out, causing the selector to match everything.
Test quarantining service example illustrating skip vs unskip as asymmetric verbs with different blast radii.
Admission webhook capping deletes at a fixed number per hour per resource kind per namespace, with bypass inside agent sessions that refuses and asks the human.

Trip wire on investigation threads per hour for a given test job failure caught a correlated infrastructure failure causing the same error signature across dozens of jobs; a one-line context update taught the agent to correlate failures before launching threads.
Feature flag service: agent owns the full canary dial from 0 to 100 and toggling off/on, but can only propose production promotion, requiring a human-held second key.
Slack loop where Malhotra asks cla tag to own the entire flag rollout loop end-to-end while he stays out of the middle, with every action stamped by the agent's own identity rather than his.
Header-spoofing example: if the agent sets its own identity header, hitting a limit simply means renaming itself and getting a fresh budget, demonstrating why stamping must be done by the proxy.
limitations: Narrowing token scope works for only about a week or two before the agent needs the verb back and a human is pressing enter by hand.
Allow lists are static guesses written up front and go stale as agent behavior changes; trip wires get better over time instead.
If the agent holds the pen on its own provenance or identity header, it can effectively claim identity itself and reset every limit.
Skipping a test can let a real bug reach production with green checks and no immediate signal.
Text-based policy is just advice with no enforcement and requires ongoing gardening as files grow.
A trip wire that nobody sees is practically useless; it pages after the breach, not before.
Prompt injection cannot talk the proxy out of a rule, but text cannot enforce either, so both layers are needed.
quantitativeClaims: Some workloads were long-running training jobs that were not checkpointed, with hours of progress lost.
Trip wire threshold was the number of investigation threads the agent launched per hour for a given test job failure, with the count clearly above baseline on the morning of the incident.
Text-based policy (a sentence in a markdown context file) works about 80% of the time.
Rate limit on the original delete incident would have capped losses at a few tens of workloads.
